correctness.rationale: Vertices with a fixed coordinate support form false-twin classes, so any resolving set must contain all but at most one vertex of every nonempty proper support class, giving the base term \(N-(2^n-2)\). For a binary coordinate, the class of support \([n]\setminus\{i\}\) is a singleton whose sole neighbor class of support \(\{i\}\) is also singleton; domination therefore forces exactly one additional landmark for each binary factor, and these forced pairs are disjoint for \(n\ge3\). The matching upper construction chooses all but one per support class and includes the required binary singleton vertices; coordinate singleton landmarks then separate every pair of omitted vertices. Fresh exhaustive searches for \((2,2,3)\) and \((2,3,3)\) independently returned the formula values \(5\) and \(8\). The frozen verifier was read and checks a wider bounded grid.
correctness.risk: The proof uses \(n\ge3\); two-factor products have separate complete-bipartite behavior.

value.rationale: The formula completes the natural mixed regime left between two published endpoint theorems and identifies exactly why \(\mathbf F_2\) is exceptional: each binary coordinate creates one unavoidable domination surcharge beyond the twin-class resolving bound. That structural explanation is reusable for related support-class graph invariants.
value.risk: The theorem does not address nonreduced finite rings or products with local nilpotents.

final_claim: For \(R=\prod_{i=1}^n\mathbf F_{q_i}\) with \(n\ge3\), the zero-divisor graph has resolving-domination number \(N-(2^n-2)+t\), where \(N\) is the number of nonzero zero-divisors and \(t\) is the number of binary field factors.
limitations: Finite direct products of fields only.
